'''Joachim "Jim" Lambek''' {{post-nominals|country=CAN|FRSC}} (5 December 1922 – 23 June 2014){{r|obit}} was a Canadian [[mathematician]]. He was Peter Redpath [[Emeritus]] [[Department of Mathematics and Statistics, McGill University|Professor of Pure Mathematics]] at [[McGill University]], where he earned his [[PhD]] degree in 1950 with [[Hans Zassenhaus]] as advisor.

== Biography ==
Lambek was born in [[Leipzig]], [[Germany]], where he attended a [[Gymnasium (Germany)|Gymnasium]].<ref name=scimeeting>{{cite conference|date=2 December 2014|conference=Faculty of Science: Meeting of Faculty|location=Montreal|url=https://www.mcgill.ca/science/files/science/facultyagendadocuments-december_2_2014-_one_file_combined_0.pdf|title=Resolution on the Death of Emeritus Professor Joachim (Jim) Lambek, Department of Mathematics and Statistics|first=Henri|last=Darmon|author-link=Henri Darmon|publisher=[[McGill University]]|page=2}}</ref> He came to England in 1938 as a [[refugee]] on the ''[[Kindertransport]]''.<ref name=obit>{{cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/montrealgazette/obituary.aspx?n=joachim-lambek&pid=171513640&fhid=14715|title=Joachim Lambek|date=27 June 2014|newspaper=Montreal Gazette|publisher=Legacy.com|access-date=31 October 2018}}</ref> From there he was interned as an [[enemy alien]] and deported to a [[List of World War II prisoner-of-war camps in Canada|prison work camp]] in [[New Brunswick]], [[Canada]]. There, he began in his spare time a mathematical apprenticeship with Fritz Rothberger, also
interned, and wrote the [[Matriculation examination|McGill Junior Matriculation]] in fall of 1941.{{r|scimeeting}} In the spring of 1942, he was released and settled in [[Montreal]], where he entered studies at McGill University, graduating with an [[Honours degree|honours]] mathematics degree in 1945 and an [[MSc]] a year later.<ref>{{cite book|page=18|editor1-first=Folkert|editor1-last=Müller-Hoissen|editor2-first=Jean Marcel|editor2-last=Pallo|editor3-first=Jim|editor3-last=Stasheff|title=Associahedra, Tamari Lattices and Related Structures|volume=299|publisher=Birkhäuser|isbn=978-3-0348-0404-2|doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-0405-9|lccn=2012942603|year=2012|series=Progress in Mathematics}}</ref> In 1950, he completed his doctorate under [[Hans Zassenhaus]] becoming McGill's first [[PhD]] in mathematics.

Lambek became assistant professor at McGill; he was made a full professor in 1963. He spent his sabbatical year 1965–66 in at the [[Institute for Mathematical Research]] at [[ETH Zurich]], where [[Beno Eckmann]] had gathered together a group of researchers interested in [[algebraic topology]] and [[category theory]], including [[Bill Lawvere]]. There Lambek reoriented his research into category theory.<ref name=lambekfest>{{cite conference|url=http://www.math.mcgill.ca/triples/lambek97/Lambek.biography.html|first=Michael|last=Barr|author-link=Michael Barr (mathematician)|title=An appreciation of Jim Lambek at McGill|date=5 December 1997|conference=LambekFest|location=Montreal}}</ref>

Lambek retired in 1992 but continued his involvement at [[Department of Mathematics and Statistics, McGill University|McGill's mathematics department]]. In 2000 a [[festschrift]] celebrating Lambek's contributions to mathematical structures in [[computer science]] was published.<ref>{{Citation | editor1-last=Barr | editor1-first=Michael | editor-link=Michael Barr (mathematician) | editor2-last=Scott | editor2-first=P. J. | editor3-last=Seely | editor3-first=R. A. G. | title=The Lambek Festschrift: mathematical structures in computer science | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | mr=1770227  | year=2000}}</ref> On the occasion of Lambek's 90th birthday, a collection ''Categories and Types in Logic, Language, and Physics'' was produced in tribute to him.<ref>{{Citation | editor1-last=Casadio| editor1-first=Claudia | editor2-last=Coeke | editor2-first=Bob | editor3-last=Moortgat| editor3-first = Michael | editor4-last=Scott | editor4-first=Philip | title=Categories and Types in Logic, Language, and Physics: Essays Dedicated to Jim Lambek on the Occasion of His 90th Birthday | publisher=Springer-Verlag | year=2014}}</ref>

== Scholarly work ==
Lambek's wrote ''two'' short PhD theses on separate topics:<ref>{{cite book | last1=Casadio | first1=Claudia| last2=Scott | first2=Philip J. | title=Joachim Lambek: The Interplay of Mathematics, Logic, and Linguistics | publisher=Springer| year=2021 | isbn=978-3-030-66545-6 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rP8kEAAAQBAJ&pg=PR13}}
</ref> one studying [[quaternions]] in the foundations of mathematical physics (specifically the [[biquaternion]] algebra containing [[Minkowski space]]), and another on the problem of embedding a [[semigroup]] into a [[group (mathematics)|group]].  The second component, attacking a question that had been [[Cancellative_semigroup#Embeddability_in_groups|previously addressed]] by [[Anatoly Maltsev]] but using a novel geometric approach, was published by the [[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Lambek | first1=J. | author1-link=Joachim Lambek | title=The immersibility of a semigroup into a group | doi=10.4153/CJM-1951-005-8 | year=1951 | journal=[[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]] | volume=3 | pages=34–43 | s2cid=124979541 | doi-access=free }}</ref> He later returned to [[biquaternion]]s when in 1995 he contributed "If Hamilton had prevailed: Quaternions in Physics", which exhibited the [[Riemann–Silberstein vector|Riemann–Silberstein]] [[bivector (complex)|bivector]] to express the free-space electromagnetic equations.

Lambek supervised 17 doctoral students, and has 99 doctoral descendants as of 2025.<ref>{{MathGenealogy}}</ref> He has over 100 publications listed in the [[Mathematical Reviews]], including 6 books.  His earlier work was mostly in [[module theory]], especially torsion theories, non-commutative localization, and [[injective module]]s.  One of his earliest papers, {{harvtxt|Lambek|Moser|1954}}, proved the [[Lambek–Moser theorem]] about integer sequences. In 1963 he published an important result, now known as Lambek's theorem, on [[character module]]s characterizing flatness of a module.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lambek|first=J.|date=1964|title=A Module is Flat if and Only if its Character Module is Injective|journal=Canadian Mathematical Bulletin|language=en|volume=7|issue=2|pages=237–243|doi=10.4153/CMB-1964-021-9|issn=0008-4395|doi-access=free}}</ref> His more recent work is in [[pregroup]]s and [[formal language]]s; his earliest works in this field were probably {{harvtxt|Lambek|1958}} and {{harvtxt|Lambek|1979}}. He is noted, among other things, for the [[Lambek calculus]], an influential effort to capture mathematical aspects of natural language syntax in logical form by reducing [[grammaticality]] to a test of logical entailment in a certain [[sequent calculus]], as well as for developing the connections between [[simply typed lambda calculus|typed lambda calculus]] and [[cartesian closed categories]] (see [[Curry–Howard–Lambek correspondence]]). His last works were on [[pregroup grammar]].
